questions.question: What is the core grouping invariant of MapReduce?
options: All intermediate values for one logical key reach one logical reducer invocation
Every mapper reads the whole input
questions.explanation: Partition and shuffle semantics bring equal keys together so the reducer can produce one logical aggregate.

questions.question: A 2,048 GiB input uses 256 MiB splits. How many mapper tasks are planned?
questions.explanation: 2,048 GiB is 2,097,152 MiB. Dividing by 256 MiB per split yields 8,192 mapper tasks.

questions.question: When is a combiner safe?
options: When partial aggregation is associative and commutative and reducer correctness does not depend on combiner execution
questions.explanation: The framework may invoke a combiner zero or multiple times, so its transformation must preserve the final result under regrouping.

questions.question: Why does adding reducers not fix one key that owns 40% of shuffle bytes?
options: Default partitioning still sends every value for that key to one reducer
questions.explanation: The logical key is indivisible under ordinary hash partitioning. Repair requires a semantic key or multi-stage aggregation change.

questions.question: What must a salted hot-key aggregation include?
options: A final merge that recombines all salted partial results for the original logical key
A different input file for every salt
questions.explanation: Salting spreads partial work, but correctness requires a second aggregation back to the original key.

questions.question: Why must retryable tasks avoid direct unprotected external side effects?
options: A failed or speculative task may execute more than once and duplicate the effect
questions.explanation: MapReduce provides task retry, not exactly-once behavior for arbitrary external systems. Effects need idempotency and reconciliation.

questions.question: What does parallelism change in a job cost model?
options: It reduces wall time but does not automatically reduce total compute or shuffle work
questions.explanation: More slots can process work concurrently, but the same bytes and records still need computation and exchange, plus coordination overhead.

questions.question: Which workload is least suited to classic MapReduce?
options: A continuous event-time stream requiring sub-second updates
A batch join over partitioned files
questions.explanation: Classic MapReduce has batch scheduling and durable phase boundaries; a streaming engine better models continuous low-latency state.
